--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Turnbull]{.doc-object-name .doc-class .doc-label .doc-label-class} | greenwood description: >- Turnbull's self-consistent NPMLE for interval-censored survival data. twitter-card: title: >- [Turnbull]{.doc-object-name .doc-class .doc-label .doc-label-class} | greenwood description: >- Turnbull's self-consistent NPMLE for interval-censored survival data. title: "[Turnbull]{.doc-object-name .doc-class .doc-label .doc-label-class}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- Turnbull's self-consistent NPMLE for interval-censored survival data. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Turnbull's self-consistent NPMLE for interval-censored survival data. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_turnbull.py#L323-L836){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-class} ```pythonsignature Turnbull( *, tol=1e-09, max_iter=10000, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Kaplan-Meier requires knowing each subject's event time exactly (up to right-censoring). When follow-up is periodic instead (clinic visits, equipment inspections), all that is known is that the event fell in a window `(lower, upper]`. Turnbull's nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator handles this directly, together with mixtures of exact, left-, right-, and interval-censored observations in the same fit. Unlike Kaplan-Meier, the NPMLE's support is not identified everywhere: the data determine a set of *maximal intersection intervals*, and only the total probability mass on each one is identified, not its placement inside. `Turnbull` reports both bounds of every such interval. Where an interval degenerates to a single point (an exact death, or a region every subject's constraint resolves unambiguously), survival is known exactly there. Otherwise it is genuinely unidentified and `~~greenwood.Turnbull.predict()`/`quantile()` return `nan` rather than interpolate. `rmst()`/`rmrl()` need a single number, so they instead fall back to Turnbull's own right-endpoint convention (every atom's mass resolves at `interval_high_`); see their docstrings for the resulting conservative (upper-bound) bias. To use this estimator, call `~~greenwood.Turnbull.fit()` with an interval-censored `Surv` response, built with `gw.Surv(time=lower, time2=upper, type="interval2")` or from a `gw.event_time()` vector via `gw.as_surv()`. With a data frame, name its columns in a formula such as `"Surv(lower, upper, type='interval2')"` and pass `data=`. Right- and left-censored responses are degenerate cases. Fitting a right-censored response through `Turnbull` reproduces `KaplanMeier` exactly, since there is then no genuine interval ambiguity. Left-truncated (counting-process) and multi-state responses are not supported. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [tol]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1e-09]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Convergence tolerance on the largest change in any atom's probability mass between EM iterations (default `1e-9`). [max_iter]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[10000]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Maximum number of EM iterations (default `10000`). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Fitted estimator]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Call `~~greenwood.Turnbull.fit()` to produce a fitted estimator with cached results (`interval_low_`, `interval_high_`, `prob_mass_`, `survival_`), accessible as aligned arrays or exported to DataFrames. ::: ## Details {.doc-details} Call `~~greenwood.Turnbull.fit` with a `Surv` response. The maximal intersection intervals are found via the Gentleman & Geyer (1994) construction: the finest partition induced by every subject's `lower`{.gd-no-link}/`upper` bounds is grouped into runs of consecutive atoms that every subject's constraint either fully includes or fully excludes (only their combined mass is identified). Probabilities on that support are then found by the EM self-consistency algorithm, which is monotone in the likelihood and converges to the NPMLE. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Six subjects observed at irregular follow-up visits, so some events are only known to lie in a window rather than at an exact time. Two are exact deaths, one is right-censored (no event observed by the last visit), and three are genuinely interval-censored: ::: {#900b554c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw # Build an interval-censored response: (lower, upper] windows, inf marks right-censoring y = gw.Surv( time=[0, 4, 7, 0, 3, 5], time2=[4, float("inf"), 7, 2.5, 6, 5], type="interval2", ) # Fit the Turnbull NPMLE tb = gw.Turnbull().fit(y) tb ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` Turnbull (self-consistent NPMLE for interval-censored data) n atoms ambiguous iters converged all 6 8 6 120 True ``` ::: ::: The fitted curve, one row per maximal intersection interval, is available via `~~greenwood.Turnbull.to_frame`: ::: {#262a2756 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} tb.to_frame(format="polars") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

Pass `by=` to fit separate curves per group (stratified analysis). ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [surv]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Surv | Outcome | str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : An interval-, right-, or left-censored `Surv` response built with `Surv()`. An `Outcome` or a formula string such as `"Surv(lower, upper, type='interval2') ~ sex"` is also accepted, with its columns read from `data`. The right-hand side names the `by` column(s). Produces one fit per unique value of `by`. Default (`None`): a single, unstratified fit. [weights]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional case weights. When `surv`{.gd-no-link} is an `Outcome` or a formula, rows with a missing value in any column used are dropped before fitting. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Turnbull]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The fitted estimator itself (for method chaining), with cached results (`interval_low_`, `interval_high_`, `prob_mass_`, `survival_`, ...) as attributes. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#97555035 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw y = gw.Surv( time=[0, 4, 7, 0, 3, 5], time2=[4, float("inf"), 7, 2.5, 6, 5], type="interval2", ) tb = gw.Turnbull().fit(y) tb.survival_ ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` array([6.66666670e-01, 6.66666670e-01, 6.66666664e-01, 6.66666664e-01, 2.22222223e-01, 2.22222223e-01, 2.22222223e-01, 1.11022302e-16]) ``` ::: ::: ### [median()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Median survival time, with its identifiability bounds, for each curve. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_turnbull.py#L594-L630){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature median( *, format=None, ) ``` ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [format]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Output format: `None` (default), `"pandas"`, `"polars"`, or `"pyarrow"`. When `None`, a backend is auto-detected (Polars, then Pandas, then PyArrow). ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [pandas.DataFrame, polars.DataFrame, or pyarrow.Table]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : One row per curve, with columns `strata`, `tau`, and `estimate`. The layout is the same for one curve (`strata` is `"all"`) as for several. ::: #### Details {.doc-details} RMST is the area under the survival curve on $[0, \tau]$. Unlike `~~greenwood.Turnbull.predict()` and `quantile()`, which report the genuine identifiability gap as `nan`, RMST needs a single number, so every atom's probability mass, ambiguous or not, is treated as resolving exactly at that atom's *right* endpoint (`interval_high_`). This is Turnbull's own convention for reporting a plottable curve from an otherwise partially-unidentified NPMLE. It is also the most conservative choice for RMST: placing mass as late as possible maximizes the area under the curve, so this reports the *largest* RMST consistent with the data, not an unbiased point estimate. There is no variance estimator for it, so no standard error or confidence limits are reported. #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#795a691a .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw y = gw.Surv( time=[0, 4, 7, 0, 3, 5], time2=[4, float("inf"), 7, 2.5, 6, 5], type="interval2", ) tb = gw.Turnbull().fit(y) tb.rmst(tau=7, format="polars") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
